records.place: Oia, Santorini PDO, Cyclades, Greece; the vineyard lies at Imerovigli

wine.name: Sigalas Kavalieros
wine.grapes: Assyrtiko alone, from vines of sixty years and more growing on their own roots.
wine.sites: Kavalieros, a single high block of old vines in the village of Imerovigli, rooted directly in the island's volcanic ash and pumice.
wine.making: The juice is fermented in stainless steel tanks at a controlled temperature. The wine then rests on its fine lees in tank for about eighteen months, stirred often in the first months and less as time passes, and it never sees oak before bottling.
wine.glass: Ripe lemon, lemon verbena and orange blossom over chalk and a strong vein of salt; creamy and full in the mouth, yet held taut by high acidity, and salty to the last.
wine.ageing: Enjoyable from the start, it is built to keep, and the house expects it to last ten years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decanting is unnecessary, though a young bottle opens with a few minutes in the glass; a generous white wine glass.

label.means: The island's Protected Designation of Origin for dry white wine of at least 85 per cent Assyrtiko.
The single vineyard block at Imerovigli from which the wine is drawn.

records.table: Kavalieros, Domaine Sigalas's single vineyard Assyrtiko, grows in one high block at Imerovigli, where own rooted vines of sixty years and more stand in volcanic ash. Eighteen months on its lees in steel give it a creamy weight around the salt and lemon; pour it with grilled fish.
records.story: The founder came from a Santorini family that, like most on the island, grew vines, and he spent the summers of his boyhood there before he trained as a mathematician, as the house's own story has it. In 1991 he bottled his first wine, a dry Santorini, at Oia in the north of the island, and the estate grew up among the vineyards of the plain there, working Assyrtiko on its own roots, since phylloxera never took hold in the ash. Beside the estate's Santorini came wines of single places, and Kavalieros was drawn from one high block of vines more than sixty years old in the village of Imerovigli. Bottled apart and given a long rest on its lees in steel rather than time in oak, it lets the site speak without wood. After a Greek investor bought a majority of the estate, its running passed in January 2020 to Kir-Yianni, the wine company of Naoussa in the north of mainland Greece, and in 2025 Kir-Yianni bought that majority itself. Kavalieros is the glass for a guest who wants to taste one named Santorini vineyard rather than a blend from many villages.

others.note: The estate's dry Santorini of Assyrtiko, the wine it first bottled in 1991.

others.name: Sigalas Vinsanto

traps: Domaine Sigalas has its cellar at Oia, but Kavalieros grows in another village, Imerovigli, so the wine is not a wine of Oia.
Kavalieros sees no oak: its creamy weight comes from about eighteen months on its fine lees in steel tanks.

records.place: Episkopi Gonia, Santorini PDO, Cyclades, Greece

wine.name: Estate Argyros Cuvée Monsignori
wine.sites: The Monsignori parcel at Episkopi Gonia, where Assyrtiko grows on its own roots, low in the island's pumice and volcanic ash, from vines the estate dates to more than two hundred years.
wine.making: Steel tanks, temperature controlled, take the fermentation; the wine then stays in them on the fine lees for most of a year, ten or eleven months by the merchants' sheets, and goes to bottle without touching oak.
wine.glass: White peach, lemon curd and beeswax over brine and wet stone; broad, dense and strong in alcohol, with firm acidity beneath and a finish of salt that lingers.
wine.ageing: Already broad within a year or two of release, it will age, the estate expects, for more than ten years.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, not colder, so that its weight shows; serve it without a decanter, in a large glass for white wine.

label.means: An old vine parcel at Episkopi Gonia, whose name the wine carries.
The island's own appellation, its dry whites led by Assyrtiko.

records.table: Estate Argyros draws Cuvée Monsignori, its old vine Assyrtiko, from one parcel at Episkopi Gonia, where ungrafted vines are counted in centuries. Raised in steel tanks on its lees, with no oak, it is broad, waxy and salty, a white to set beside octopus.
records.story: Vines have been the Argyros family's work on Santorini since the eighteenth century, the estate says, and it dates itself to 1903, when its founder began making wine under the family's name at Episkopi Gonia. Its vineyards hold old vines on their own roots, many never replanted, for the island's volcanic soil gave phylloxera no foothold. In 1974 a new head of the family took over, and the estate's standing rose under him, as the estate's own history and other accounts have it. The fourth generation followed, and in the 2010s the estate moved into a new winery that keeps the old cellars and the press of 1903 beside it. Cuvée Monsignori comes from the parcel of that name at Episkopi, from vines the estate dates to more than two centuries, made as a white of one place and raised on its lees without oak. From the harvest of 2021 the estate released no Monsignori at all, by its own announcement, and the cuvée returned with the next vintage. Weight, wax and salt are what vines two centuries old give on Santorini, and a glass of Monsignori holds all three.

Santorini's vines grow ungrafted because phylloxera cannot live in the volcanic ash, not because of any quarantine.

wine.name: Gaia Thalassitis
wine.sites: Old vines of seventy to eighty years in the villages of Episkopi, Akrotiri and Pyrgos, on volcanic soils of ash and pumice, with yields kept low.
wine.making: The chilled, destemmed grapes rest about twelve hours on their skins at around 10 degrees Celsius. Selected yeasts then ferment the juice at 16 to 17 degrees Celsius in stainless steel tanks, with no malolactic fermentation, and the wine is kept in steel, untouched by oak, until bottling.
wine.glass: Lime zest, grapefruit and lemon over meadow herbs and a faint note of tobacco; dry and taut, all high, cutting acidity, ending long and salty.
wine.ageing: Bright and ready on release; the house suggests two to three years in the cellar, which soften its edge as honey and riper fruit come through.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; skip the decanter; a white wine glass of middling size.

label.means: Of the sea, in Greek: a name tied in accounts to the ancient habit of mixing wine with sea water.
The appellation of the island, which asks a dry white for at least 85 per cent Assyrtiko.

records.table: Thalassitis was Gaia's first wine, a Santorini Assyrtiko from old vines in three villages, fermented cool and kept in steel with no oak. Taut, lemony and salty, it is the island's plain style, made for oysters or feta and poured cold.
records.story: Two agronomists founded Gaia in 1994, and its first wine was Thalassitis, a dry Santorini of Assyrtiko, the house relates. Its name means of the sea, and accounts tie it to an ancient Greek habit of mixing wine with sea water. The Santorini winery took over a stone tomato factory built early in the twentieth century on the beach at Exo Gonia, on the island's east coast, which had made purée from the island's small tomatoes until it closed in the 1970s. In 1997 the partners built a second winery among their own vineyards at Koutsi in Nemea, on the Peloponnese, for Agiorgitiko, so that one house speaks for both the island and the mainland. On Santorini they went on to ferment Assyrtiko wild, on its own yeasts, in steel, oak and acacia, and from 2009 they lowered bottles of Thalassitis into the sea off the island to age, an echo of the name. Thalassitis itself stayed the plain style, fermented cool and kept from wood. It shows Santorini Assyrtiko as the island gives it, before oak or long lees change it.

others.note: Santorini Assyrtiko fermented by wild yeasts in steel tanks and in French oak, American oak and acacia barrels.

traps: Thalassitis is the unoaked one; the house's oaked Assyrtiko is the Wild Ferment, and its oak fermented Thalassitis was renamed Nykteri in 2019.

wine.name: Hatzidakis Nykteri
wine.sites: Vineyards at Megalochori: old, ungrafted Assyrtiko in the island's volcanic soil.
wine.making: Hand picked and overripe, the grapes spend a night in the cold, then are destemmed and given twelve hours on their skins. The juice ferments with its own yeasts at 17 to 18 degrees Celsius, and the wine matures about twelve months in French oak barrels of several sizes before it is bottled unfiltered.
wine.glass: Baked apple, preserved lemon and toasted almond over honey, smoke and a breath of sea air; golden, full and broad, with Assyrtiko's acidity keeping the weight fresh.
wine.ageing: Closed in its youth, it unfolds slowly in bottle, and the house gives it more than ten years.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; a young bottle that seems closed gains from time in a decanter; a large white wine glass.

label.means: Night work: a dry Santorini of at least 13.5 per cent alcohol, aged at least three months in oak.
The Protected Designation of Origin under which Nykteri is made as a named style.

records.table: Hatzidakis Nykteri is the riper, oaked style of Santorini, named for the night pressing: the overripe grapes of old Assyrtiko vines at Megalochori, wild fermented and aged a year in French oak. Broad and nutty with a salty spine, it suits lobster or roast pork.
records.story: Nykteri means night work: grapes picked for it were pressed during the night after the harvest, and the name came to mean a riper dry wine of Santorini, aged in oak, by the account of the national wine body. The house began with an oenologist born on Crete, who came to the island in 1991 to work at the Boutari winery there and rose to be its chief oenologist, and his wife, who ran that winery's hospitality. Her family's vineyard at Pyrgos, abandoned since her parents left the island after the earthquake of 1956, became their own, and in a cave at its end he made a small cellar. The first bottles, a dry Santorini and a red Mavrotragano of the 1997 vintage, were released in 1998, the house records. The house farmed its vineyard organically and had it certified. In 2000 it bought a vineyard above a larger cave for its Vinsanto, and in 2016 it moved to a cellar on the road from Pyrgos to Emporio. The founder died in 2017, and his family took the house on. Its Nykteri shows a guest that Santorini can be rich and oaked and yet taste of salt.

The founder, Haridimos Hatzidakis, died in August 2017 in two accounts (one says May 2017, one 2016); his year of birth was found in none, so he is described, not named, and the house keeps its name.

His widow, who founded the house with him, and their eldest daughter, who directs it, are living and never named; Konstantina Chryssou and Stella Hatzidaki are not yet in people.json and should be added.
Founded 1997 rests on the house's own pages (a cave winery since 1997, first bottles of the 1997 vintage released in 1998); one critic's site gives 1996 and one merchant 1999 for the first bottles.

The plan's why says the founder revived the island's Nykteri; no source said so and the record does not. The house's claim that its vineyard was the first on Santorini certified organic rests on the house alone and is left out; the story says only that it was farmed organically and certified.

Organic farming for the Nykteri's own vineyards is said by one merchant and denied by another for a recent vintage, so the wine fields leave it out; the vineyards at Megalochori are the house's page with two merchants beside it.
The pick stands: the house's dry Santorinis are as well known, but Nykteri is the wine of the style the plan asks to teach, and the house names it on its own page.

wine.name: Santo Vinsanto
wine.grapes: Assyrtiko, the great majority, with Aidani.
wine.sites: Grapes from the union's member growers across the island, own rooted vines in Santorini's volcanic soil.
wine.making: Picked in late August, the grapes are laid in the sun to dry for six to ten days, then fermented slowly over forty to sixty days. The wine is aged for years in oak barrels before bottling, three years in used 225 litre barrels for the 2020 vintage.
wine.glass: Dried apricot, raisin and fig over cinnamon, clove and caramel; deep amber, thick and sweet, yet cut by a fine thread of acidity that keeps it from cloying.
wine.ageing: Long lived, though ready the day it is released; the union also bottles selections after twelve and twenty years of ageing, darker and turned towards coffee and dates.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no decanter is needed; small measures in a small dessert wine glass.

label.means: Santorini's sweet wine of sun dried grapes, at least 51 per cent Assyrtiko, aged at least two years.
An appellation that covers the island's sweet Vinsanto as well as its dry whites.

records.table: Sun dried for a week or more, then fermented slowly and aged years in oak, Assyrtiko and Aidani become Santo Vinsanto, the sweet wine of Santorini's growers' union. It tastes of apricot, raisin and cinnamon, kept lively by its acidity; serve it cool, in small glasses, after dinner.
records.story: In 1911, as the union's own history has it, the Santorini Vine and Wine Protection Fund was set up for the island's growers, the body from which Santo Wines grew. In 1947 it became the Union of Santorini Cooperatives, formed to process, export and promote the island's produce, above all its wine. Its members are the island's smallholders, whose grapes it takes in and makes into dry whites and the sweet Vinsanto. In 1992 the union completed a new winery in the village of Pyrgos. For Vinsanto, the sweet wine of grapes dried in the sun after the August harvest, the turning point came in 2002, when, by the union's timeline, European law brought Vinsanto under the Santorini appellation; other accounts add that the island gained sole use of the one word name, while Italy kept Vin Santo, two words, for its own. The union's Vinsanto carries its vintage and spends years in oak, and older bottlings are held for a decade or two more before release. Santo's Vinsanto is the ready answer to a request for Santorini's sweet wine, its sweetness owed to the sun rather than to added spirit.

traps: Santorini Vinsanto, one word, is sun dried Assyrtiko from the island; Tuscan Vin Santo, two words, is made from other grapes dried indoors.
Santo's Vinsanto owes its sweetness to grapes dried in the sun before fermenting, not to added grape spirit: the union makes it as a naturally sweet wine.
Santo Wines is the island's union of cooperatives, not a family estate.

cards.front: Santo Wines: when and where did the union complete its new winery?
What did Santo Wines become in 1947, and what had it been since 1911?
cards.back: The Union of Santorini Cooperatives; before that, the Santorini Vine and Wine Protection Fund.

questions.q: Which rule of the Santorini appellation must a Vinsanto such as Santo's meet?
opts: Sun dried grapes and at least two years of ageing
Frozen grapes pressed in the depth of winter
Grape spirit added to stop the fermentation
Grapes shrivelled by noble rot on the vine
questions.exp: Vinsanto comes from sun dried grapes, at least 51 per cent Assyrtiko, and needs at least 24 months of ageing; added spirit is no part of that rule, and neither frost nor noble rot plays a part.

questions.q: In 2002 European law brought Santorini's sweet wine of sun dried grapes under the island's appellation. By which name?
opts: Vinsanto
Nykteri
Liastos
Vin Santo
questions.exp: Vinsanto, one word, came under the Santorini appellation in 2002; Vin Santo, two words, is Italy's own, and Nykteri is the island's oaked dry style.

report: Searches for this record: three of the group's 35, two restricted to santowines.gr, with one of Wikipedia for 1947 and 2002; the appellation's rules are the Wines of Greece page, read for the whole group in two more searches.
The union dates itself to 1911 in its first form; founded keeps the plan's and the region record's 1947, the year it became the Union, in the union's own timeline and Wikipedia.

The fact sheets differ by vintage on drying (six to eight days, eight to ten) and on time in oak (three years in small barrels for one vintage, six in another passage), so the record says a week to ten days and years in oak.
The grape shares (about 85 per cent Assyrtiko, 15 Aidani) are one vintage's sheet and are told as the great majority.
The Venetian and Ottoman history of Vinsanto and the story of the name rest on Wikipedia alone and are left out; so the story tells no history of the wine before the ruling of 2002.

changed: wine.making: the drying is six to ten days (the union's sheets give six to eight, its twenty year page eight to ten) and the slow fermentation forty to sixty days, no longer six to eight weeks; the three years of the 2020 vintage are in used 225 litre barrels, by the union's sheet. The card follows.
wine.ageing: the union bottles selections after twelve and twenty years of ageing, a 2002 vintage bottled in 2023 among them, no longer vintages after more than twenty years in oak.

story and questions[1]: 2002 is the year European law brought Vinsanto under the Santorini appellation, by the union's own timeline; the sole use of the one word name, and Italy's two word Vin Santo, are told as other accounts, since the instrument of 2002 is given three ways (a European ruling, a Greek ministerial decision, the appellation's extension).

story, traps[1] and questions[0].exp: never fortified is no longer said of Vinsanto in general, since the appellation's specification also provides a liqueur wine of sun dried grapes made with added alcohol; the union's own pages call its Vinsanto naturally sweet, and the record now says that of Santo's wine.
others[0]: the 12 Years Ageing is a selection of vintages (2008, 2009 and 2010 for one bottling) held at least twelve years in French oak, by the union's page.
open: Whether the appellation's liqueur wine of sun dried grapes may carry the word Vinsanto was not settled; the record no longer depends on it.
The union's pages differ on time in oak for the standard bottling (thirty six months on the wine page, three years for 2020, six years for 2016); the record keeps years in oak with the 2020 figure.
